questions.question: What is connection pooling and why is it critical for production Java applications?
questions.title: Connection Pooling in JDBC — Why It Is Critical
questions.direct_answer: **Connection pooling** pre-creates a set of database connections and reuses them. Creating a connection costs 20-100ms (TCP + auth). A pool eliminates this overhead for every request. Without pooling, a high-traffic application cannot scale.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of why connection pooling exists
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing the cost of creating a raw database connection
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Quantify: 100 requests/second times 50ms per connection creation equals the application being unable to handle the load

sections.title: Why Connection Pooling?
sections.content: Creating a JDBC connection involves: DNS resolution, TCP three-way handshake, TLS negotiation (if HTTPS), database authentication, and session setup. This can take 20-100ms. For a web app with 100 concurrent users, creating one connection per request is unsustainable.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Pool creates N connections at startup (typically 5-20)
- Request borrows a connection, uses it, returns it to pool
- If no connection available: request waits up to connectionTimeout
- HikariCP: Spring Boot default — fastest Java connection pool
- Pool monitors connections: removes stale connections, validates before lending
- Reduces connection count to database: 100 threads can share 10 pool connections

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Connection pooling is essential because creating a database connection is expensive. Each new connection requires TCP handshake, authentication, and session setup — which takes 20 to 100 milliseconds. For an application handling 100 requests per second, creating a new connection for each request would add 2-10 seconds of latency. A connection pool solves this by maintaining a set of ready-to-use connections. When a request needs the database, it borrows a connection from the pool, uses it, then returns it. The pool pre-warms connections at startup and maintains them. HikariCP is the standard connection pool in Spring Boot applications.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java 17 app connecting to a MySQL database with JDBC to query an orders table
speakable_v2.hook: Creating a database connection from scratch on every request is like renting a car for every trip across town — pooling keeps a fleet waiting in the garage.

beats.text: Connection pooling maintains a set of pre-created, ready-to-use database connections. When a request needs the database, it borrows a connection from the pool, uses it, then returns it. The pool recycles it for the next request rather than destroying and re-creating it.

It exists because creating a JDBC connection is expensive — it requires a TCP handshake, TLS negotiation, database authentication, and session setup. That costs 20 to 100 milliseconds per connection. At 100 requests per second, that overhead alone saturates your response budget.

items: Startup: pool creates N connections (typically 5–20) before the first request arrives
Borrow: request thread calls getConnection() — pool hands out an idle connection immediately
Return: after the try-with-resources block closes the connection, it goes back to the pool, not to the database
Wait: if all connections are in use, the thread waits up to connectionTimeout before throwing an exception

beats.text: Our orders app starts with 10 HikariCP connections to MySQL. When 10 concurrent requests query the orders table simultaneously, each gets a connection instantly — zero TCP overhead. The 11th request waits milliseconds until one is returned. Without pooling, each of those 10 requests would spend ~50ms just establishing a connection before running the query. [depth: how the pool manages the borrow-return lifecycle internally]

items: Not closing connections — they don't return to the pool, gradually exhausting it until the app can't reach the database
Setting pool size too high — the database server has finite CPU; 200 simultaneous connections hurt more than they help
Using DriverManager.getConnection() directly in production code without a pool — fine for local testing, a performance disaster under real load

questions.question: What is HikariCP and how do you configure it in Spring Boot?
questions.title: HikariCP Configuration in Spring Boot
questions.direct_answer: **HikariCP** is the fastest Java connection pool and Spring Boot's default. Configure it via `spring.datasource.hikari.*` properties in `application.properties`. Key settings: `maximum-pool-size` (default 10), `minimum-idle`, `connection-timeout`, `idle-timeout`.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing default pool size is 10 or that connection-timeout is 30 seconds by default
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the practical meaning of each key property and how to tune them for your application

sections.title: HikariCP Configuration in application.properties
sections.content:
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/mydb
spring.datasource.username=user
spring.datasource.password=pass

# HikariCP settings
spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size=20
spring.datasource.hikari.minimum-idle=5
spring.datasource.hikari.connection-timeout=30000
spring.datasource.hikari.idle-timeout=600000
spring.datasource.hikari.max-lifetime=1800000

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- maximum-pool-size: max connections in pool (default: 10)
- minimum-idle: min idle connections maintained (default: same as max)
- connection-timeout: ms to wait for connection from pool (default: 30000ms)
- idle-timeout: ms an idle connection can stay before removal (default: 600000ms)
- max-lifetime: max lifetime of a connection in pool (default: 1800000ms = 30min)
- HikariCP auto-selected by Spring Boot when hikari JAR is on classpath

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: HikariCP is the default connection pool in Spring Boot — it is included automatically when you add a database dependency. You configure it through application.properties using the spring.datasource.hikari prefix. The most important setting is maximum-pool-size which defaults to 10. If your application needs more concurrent database connections, you increase this. The connection-timeout setting controls how long a thread waits for a connection before throwing an exception — defaults to 30 seconds. The max-lifetime prevents the pool from holding connections longer than the database server's connection timeout — important to avoid stale connection errors.

beats.text: HikariCP is Spring Boot's default JDBC connection pool — it's automatically included when you add spring-boot-starter-data-jpa or spring-boot-starter-jdbc. You configure it through application.properties using the spring.datasource.hikari prefix, and Spring Boot's auto-configuration wires it up without any boilerplate bean code.

It's the default because it's consistently the fastest Java connection pool in benchmarks, with a minimal footprint and excellent production reliability. Knowing its key properties means you can tune it confidently instead of guessing at defaults.

items: maximum-pool-size (default 10): the hard ceiling on connections; increase this if threads wait for connections under peak load
minimum-idle (default = max): how many idle connections to keep warm; lower it to reduce DB server load during quiet periods
connection-timeout (default 30000ms): how long a thread waits for a connection before throwing an exception
idle-timeout (default 600000ms): how long an unused connection stays in the pool before being closed
max-lifetime (default 1800000ms): maximum age of any connection; prevents stale connections when the DB server recycles them server-side

beats.text: For our orders app we set maximum-pool-size=20 because load testing showed 10 connections caused thread waits at peak. We set max-lifetime=1740000 (29 minutes) because our MySQL server has wait_timeout=1800 — this ensures HikariCP retires connections just before MySQL closes them server-side, avoiding stale connection errors. [depth: how max-lifetime prevents connections from outliving the database server's own session timeout]

items: Leaving max-lifetime above the database server's wait_timeout causes 'connection was closed by server' errors in production
Setting maximum-pool-size to the number of web server threads — more connections than the DB can handle efficiently actually slows queries
Not setting minimum-idle to a lower value than max means the pool keeps 20 connections open even at 3am when load is near zero

questions.question: What happens when all connections in a pool are in use?
questions.title: Connection Pool Exhaustion in JDBC
questions.direct_answer: When all pool connections are in use, new requests **wait** for a connection up to `connectionTimeout` (default 30 seconds). After the timeout, a `SQLTimeoutException` or `ConnectionAcquisitionException` is thrown. Pool exhaustion indicates the pool is undersized or connections are being held too long.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of pool exhaustion scenarios and remedies
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing what happens at timeout or how to diagnose pool exhaustion
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention common causes: long transactions, connection leaks, undersized pool, and how to detect via monitoring

sections.title: Pool Exhaustion Behavior
sections.content: When a request needs a connection and all pool connections are borrowed, the request enters a wait queue. If a connection becomes available before connectionTimeout, the request proceeds normally. If the timeout elapses, an exception is thrown and the request fails.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Pool exhausted: requests queue up waiting for a connection
- After connectionTimeout (default 30s): SQLTimeoutException thrown
- Common causes: pool too small, long-running transactions, connection leaks
- Connection leak: transaction/connection opened but never closed
- Fix: increase pool size, fix connection leaks, optimize slow queries
- HikariCP has leak-detection-threshold property to find leaks

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: When all connections in the pool are checked out, new requests wait in a queue for a connection to be returned. HikariCP waits up to the connection-timeout setting, which defaults to 30 seconds. If no connection becomes available in that time, an exception is thrown. Pool exhaustion can happen for several reasons: the pool is too small for the load, connections are being held for too long by slow queries or long transactions, or there is a connection leak where code checks out a connection but does not return it. HikariCP has a leak-detection-threshold property that logs a warning if a connection is held longer than a specified time, which helps diagnose leaks.

seo.metaTitle: Connection Pool Exhaustion in JDBC | Java Backend Interview

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java 17 app connecting to a MySQL database with JDBC to query an orders table
speakable_v2.hook: Pool exhaustion doesn't crash your app immediately — it queues threads and then throws, which is almost worse to debug.

beats.text: Pool exhaustion is when every connection in the pool is currently checked out and a new request needs one. The requesting thread doesn't fail immediately — it joins a wait queue. If a connection is returned quickly, the thread continues normally. If not, it times out and throws an exception.

It exists as a safety valve. Throwing after a timeout is better than waiting forever and freezing threads indefinitely, or silently returning a null connection. The exception surfaces the problem so you can diagnose and fix the root cause.

items: All connections checked out — thread enters wait queue immediately
Connection returned within connectionTimeout (30s default) — thread unblocks and proceeds
Timeout reached with no free connection — HikariCP throws SQLTransientConnectionException
Root causes: pool undersized for traffic, slow queries holding connections, or connection leaks never returning connections

beats.text: Our orders app has maximum-pool-size=10. A slow reporting query holds 10 connections for 35 seconds. The 11th order request waits 30 seconds and then gets SQLTransientConnectionException: connection is not available. Setting leak-detection-threshold=5000 in application.properties makes HikariCP log a warning with stack trace for any connection held longer than 5 seconds — which fingers the slow report immediately. [depth: how HikariCP tracks acquisition time per connection to generate leak warnings]

items: Increasing pool size to fix exhaustion without diagnosing the cause — a leak will just exhaust the larger pool more slowly
Setting connectionTimeout too high — threads pile up for 5 minutes before failing, consuming server memory the whole time
Not enabling leak-detection-threshold in development — connection leaks that show up in production were silently present all along

speakable_v2.cap: When you see pool exhaustion in logs, check three things in order: connection leaks (HikariCP warnings), slow queries holding connections too long, and then pool size relative to concurrency.

questions.question: What is a connection leak in JDBC and how do you prevent it?
questions.title: Connection Leaks in JDBC — Prevention and Detection
questions.direct_answer: A **connection leak** occurs when a database connection is checked out from the pool but never returned (not closed). Leaks exhaust the pool over time, causing application failures. Prevent with try-with-resources; detect with HikariCP's `leak-detection-threshold`.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not using try-with-resources and relying on finally blocks that might also throw exceptions
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain leak detection threshold and mention that Spring JdbcTemplate eliminates leaks entirely by managing connections

sections.title: Connection Leak Example and Fix
Key Points
sections.content:
- Connection leak: borrowed from pool, never returned
- Cause: exception thrown before close(), no finally block
- Prevention: always use try-with-resources
- HikariCP leak-detection-threshold: logs warning if connection held longer than N ms
- Spring JdbcTemplate: manages connections automatically — no leaks possible
- Leak symptom: pool gradually exhausts, application slows, eventually fails

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: A connection leak happens when your code borrows a connection from the pool but never returns it — usually because an exception is thrown before the close call is reached. Leaked connections accumulate over time and eventually exhaust the pool. The primary prevention is always using try-with-resources, which guarantees the connection is closed no matter what happens. For detecting leaks, HikariCP has a leak-detection-threshold setting — if a connection is held longer than that many milliseconds, HikariCP logs a warning with the stack trace of where it was acquired. Using Spring JdbcTemplate or Spring Data JPA eliminates this concern entirely because they manage connection lifecycle automatically.

seo.metaTitle: Connection Leaks in JDBC — Prevention | Java Backend Interview
seo.metaDescription: Learn about JDBC connection leaks, how to prevent them with try-with-resources and detect them with HikariCP. Java fresher interview question.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java 17 app connecting to a MySQL database with JDBC to query an orders table
speakable_v2.hook: A connection leak is a slow death — the pool drains one abandoned connection at a time until the app stops talking to the database.

beats.text: A connection leak happens when code checks out a connection from the pool and never returns it — usually because an exception fires before the close() call is reached. The pool doesn't know the connection is gone; it just sees one fewer available connection. Over time these accumulate and exhaust the pool.

It exists because pre-try-with-resources JDBC code required explicit finally blocks, and finally blocks themselves could throw exceptions that swallowed the close() call. It's easy to get wrong under error conditions, and the symptom — gradual pool shrinkage — takes hours to show up.

items: Cause: exception thrown between getConnection() and conn.close(), with no try-with-resources protecting the close
Symptom: pool size shrinks slowly; connection wait times grow; SQLTransientConnectionException starts appearing hours or days later
Prevention: always open connections inside try-with-resources — Java guarantees close() runs even on exception or return
Detection: set spring.datasource.hikari.leak-detection-threshold=5000; HikariCP logs the acquisition stack trace for any connection held longer than 5 seconds

beats.text: Our orders app had a query method that returned early on a null check before closing the ResultSet and Connection. Every null-order request leaked one connection. After 10 requests the pool was dry. Wrapping the whole block in try (Connection conn = ds.getConnection(); PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement(sql)) fixed it — Java closes both automatically. [depth: how AutoCloseable.close() is guaranteed by the JVM regardless of exception path]

items: Relying on finally instead of try-with-resources — if the finally block itself throws, close() gets skipped
Not setting leak-detection-threshold in development — leaks that only show up under production load are invisible until the outage
Using JdbcTemplate handles this entirely — it never leaks because Spring owns the connection lifecycle, so prefer it when writing new code

speakable_v2.cap: Try-with-resources for raw JDBC, or use JdbcTemplate and let Spring manage the lifecycle — either way, your pool stays healthy.

questions.question: How do you choose the right connection pool size?
questions.title: Choosing Connection Pool Size
questions.direct_answer: Pool size depends on: number of concurrent threads, query duration, and database capacity. A common formula: `pool size = Tn × (Cm - 1) + 1` (Tn = thread count, Cm = concurrent DB calls per thread). HikariCP recommends starting with `(CPU cores × 2) + disk spindles` for OLTP.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Setting pool size = thread count without considering query concurrency patterns
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Reference HikariCP's recommendation and explain why too large a pool can hurt database performance

sections.title: Pool Sizing Guidelines
sections.content: More connections is not always better. The database server has CPU limits — too many concurrent queries degrade performance for all. HikariCP's guidance: for OLTP workloads, start with CPU cores times 2 plus disk spindles. Measure and tune based on actual load.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Too small: threads wait, latency increases
- Too large: database overloaded with concurrent queries, all slow down
- HikariCP recommendation for OLTP: (CPU cores * 2) + disk spindles
- Default of 10 is a good starting point for most apps
- Monitor: pool wait time, pool utilization, query latency
- Load test to find the right size for your specific workload

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Pool sizing is a balance between having enough connections so threads do not wait, and not overloading the database with too many concurrent queries. HikariCP recommends starting with CPU cores times 2 plus disk spindles as a baseline for OLTP applications. The default of 10 connections works well for many applications. Too large a pool is actually harmful — the database server has finite CPU, and 100 simultaneous queries compete with each other and all slow down. The right approach is to start with the default, monitor connection wait times and database CPU, and tune from there. For a 4-core database server, 10-20 pool connections is often right.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java 17 app connecting to a MySQL database with JDBC to query an orders table
speakable_v2.hook: More connections sound like more capacity — but past a point you're just adding traffic jams on the database side.

beats.text: The goal is the sweet spot where threads never wait for a connection but the database server isn't drowning in concurrent queries. Too small and your threads queue; too large and the database's CPU is overloaded and all queries slow down together.

items: Start with the default (10) — works well for most single-instance OLTP apps with a reasonably fast database
Use HikariCP's formula: (CPU cores × 2) + disk spindles — for a 4-core SSD database server, that's about 9
Match to observed load: if Spring Boot Actuator shows hikaricp.connections.pending > 0 consistently, increase pool size

beats.text: A small pool saves database resources but causes thread wait times under load. A large pool eliminates waits but overloads the database server — all queries compete for CPU and disk I/O simultaneously, making each individual query slower. The database is the bottleneck, not the pool size.

Start at 10. Load test with realistic traffic. If hikaricp.connections.pending appears in metrics, increase by 5 at a time and re-test. If database CPU hits 80%+ under normal load, reduce pool size. For a 4-core MySQL server handling typical OLTP, 10–20 is almost always the right range.

items: You're running multiple app instances pointing to the same database — each has its own pool, so total connections = instances × pool size; multiply accordingly
Your workload is mostly long-running reports rather than fast OLTP queries — report queries hold connections much longer, so you need a separate DataSource for reporting with its own smaller pool

questions.title: Connection Pool Exhaustion
questions.direct_answer: When all connections are checked out, new requests wait in a queue until a connection is returned. If the wait exceeds the configured timeout (e.g., HikariCP's connectionTimeout, default 30s), a SQLException is thrown.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of what pool exhaustion means and how to handle it
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking the application crashes immediately instead of waiting then throwing an exception
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention monitoring metrics like pool pending count and how to tune pool size to prevent exhaustion

sections.title: What Happens During Pool Exhaustion
sections.content:
When all connections are borrowed and a new request arrives:
1. Request waits in a queue for a connection to be returned
2. If a connection is returned within connectionTimeout (default 30 seconds in HikariCP), the waiting thread gets it
3. If no connection is returned in time, HikariCP throws `SQLTransientConnectionException: connection is not available`

**Symptoms of pool exhaustion:**
- High latency for DB operations
- Timeout errors in logs
- Pool pending count metric increasing

**Prevention:**
- Increase pool size (but not blindly — test with load)
- Reduce query duration (optimize slow queries)
- Ensure connections are always closed (use try-with-resources)
- Use Spring's `@Transactional` correctly to avoid holding connections too long

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Requests queue up, not fail immediately
- connectionTimeout controls how long threads wait (default 30s in HikariCP)
- Throws SQLTransientConnectionException after timeout
- Common cause: connection leaks (not closing connections)
- Prevention: try-with-resources, optimize slow queries, tune pool size
- Monitor: hikaricp.connections.pending metric

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: When all connections are checked out, new database requests don't fail immediately — they queue up and wait for a connection to become available. HikariCP has a connectionTimeout setting, defaulting to 30 seconds. If a connection is freed within that window, the waiting thread gets it and proceeds normally. If 30 seconds pass without a free connection, HikariCP throws a SQLTransientConnectionException. The most common cause of pool exhaustion in real applications is connection leaks — code that borrows a connection but never returns it, for example, not closing a ResultSet or Connection in a finally block. Using try-with-resources guarantees the connection is returned to the pool even if an exception occurs. You can also watch for exhaustion in production by monitoring the hikaricp.connections.pending metric.

The queuing behavior exists to handle brief traffic spikes gracefully. A burst of requests might briefly exceed pool capacity but resolve in milliseconds when fast queries return their connections. Waiting is better than rejecting; throwing after timeout is better than waiting forever.

questions.question: What is the difference between connectionTimeout and idleTimeout in HikariCP?
questions.title: HikariCP connectionTimeout vs idleTimeout
questions.direct_answer: connectionTimeout is how long a client thread waits to borrow a connection from the pool. idleTimeout is how long an idle (unused) connection sits in the pool before being closed and removed to free database resources.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing connectionTimeout (client wait) with connection timeout to database server
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Also mention maxLifetime (total connection age) and its importance for preventing stale connections

sections.title: HikariCP Key Timeouts
sections.content:
**connectionTimeout (default: 30,000 ms)**
- How long a thread waits for a connection to become available from the pool
- If no connection is available within this time → throws SQLException
- Client-side wait time

**idleTimeout (default: 600,000 ms = 10 minutes)**
- How long a connection can remain idle in the pool before being evicted
- Helps shrink the pool under low load
- Only applies when pool size > minimumIdle

**maxLifetime (default: 1,800,000 ms = 30 minutes)**
- Maximum lifetime of a connection regardless of usage
- Connections are retired and recreated before they exceed this age
- Critical for databases that close connections server-side after a period
- Set this a few seconds less than the database's wait_timeout

**keepaliveTime**
- Sends a keepalive query to test idle connections
- Prevents them from being closed by firewalls or DB server

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- connectionTimeout: client waits this long to get a connection from pool
- idleTimeout: idle connections evicted after this time (frees DB resources)
- maxLifetime: all connections recycled at this age (prevents stale connections)
- maxLifetime should be slightly less than DB server's connection timeout
- minimumIdle + maximumPoolSize control pool size range
- Set these in application.properties: spring.datasource.hikari.*

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: These two timeouts serve completely different purposes. connectionTimeout controls how long your application thread waits when it requests a connection but all connections are busy. The default is 30 seconds. If no connection is freed in that window, you get a SQLException. idleTimeout is about the pool cleaning up unused connections. When traffic is low and connections sit idle for longer than idleTimeout — default 10 minutes — HikariCP closes and removes them from the pool. This helps release database server resources when the application isn't busy. There is also maxLifetime, which I consider the most important one: every connection is recycled after 30 minutes regardless of use. This prevents stale connections — database servers like MySQL close connections after their own wait_timeout, and without maxLifetime, HikariCP would keep trying to use dead connections.

speakable_v2.hook: These two sound similar but measure completely different things — one is about your threads waiting, the other is about the pool doing housekeeping.

items.text: How long your application thread waits when it requests a connection and none are immediately available. It's client-side blocking time. Default is 30 seconds. If the pool is exhausted and no connection is freed in time, HikariCP throws SQLTransientConnectionException.

How long an unused connection can sit in the pool before HikariCP closes it and removes it. It's pool housekeeping. Default is 10 minutes. Helps shrink the pool during low-traffic periods so you're not holding open database connections the app doesn't need.

values: Thread wait for a connection to become available
How long an unused connection sits idle in the pool
Pool cleanup — which connections to close

beats.text: Also worth knowing: maxLifetime (default 30 minutes) is arguably the most critical — every connection is recycled at this age regardless of use. Set it slightly below your database server's wait_timeout to prevent HikariCP from trying to use connections the database has already closed server-side.

At 3am our orders app is quiet; 9 of 10 connections are idle. After 10 minutes (idleTimeout) HikariCP closes those 9, keeping only minimumIdle connections alive. At 9am when traffic surges, a request waits a few milliseconds for HikariCP to open new connections — that brief pause is connectionTimeout at work (well under the 30-second limit).

speakable_v2.cap: connectionTimeout = 'how long I wait to get one', idleTimeout = 'how long the pool keeps unused ones'. Both are tunable; maxLifetime is the third you should always check.

questions.question: How does Spring Boot auto-configure a connection pool?
questions.title: Spring Boot Connection Pool Auto-Configuration
questions.direct_answer: Spring Boot auto-configures HikariCP (the default pool) when spring-boot-starter-data-jpa or spring-boot-starter-jdbc is on the classpath. You only need to set spring.datasource.url, username, and password in application.properties.

interviewer_intent.testing: Spring Boot auto-configuration awareness and practical setup knowledge
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Manually creating a DataSource bean when Spring Boot can do it automatically
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that you can tune HikariCP via spring.datasource.hikari.* and switch pools by excluding HikariCP

sections.title: Spring Boot DataSource Auto-Configuration
sections.content:
Spring Boot's DataSourceAutoConfiguration class detects the classpath and creates a DataSource bean automatically.

**Default pool priority:**
1. HikariCP (preferred, fastest)
2. Apache Tomcat Pool (if Hikari not present)
3. Commons DBCP2 (fallback)

**Minimal configuration (application.properties):**
```properties
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/mydb
spring.datasource.username=root
spring.datasource.password=secret
spring.datasource.driver-class-name=com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver
```

**Tuning HikariCP:**
```properties
spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size=10
spring.datasource.hikari.connection-timeout=30000
spring.datasource.hikari.idle-timeout=600000
spring.datasource.hikari.max-lifetime=1800000
spring.datasource.hikari.pool-name=MyAppPool
```

**Override with custom DataSource bean:**
Annotate with @Bean and @Primary if you need custom logic

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- spring-boot-starter-data-jpa pulls in HikariCP by default
- Just set spring.datasource.url/username/password — pool is auto-created
- Tune with spring.datasource.hikari.* properties
- spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size is the most common tuning knob
- @Bean DataSource overrides auto-configuration if needed
- Spring Boot Actuator exposes pool metrics at /actuator/metrics/hikaricp.connections

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Spring Boot makes connection pool setup very straightforward. When you include spring-boot-starter-data-jpa or spring-boot-starter-jdbc in your pom.xml, HikariCP is pulled in automatically. Spring Boot's DataSourceAutoConfiguration detects HikariCP on the classpath and creates a DataSource bean with a connection pool. All you need to provide is the database URL, username, and password in application.properties. You can tune the pool by adding spring.datasource.hikari properties — for example, setting maximum-pool-size to 20 or adjusting connection-timeout. In a production app I worked on, we set maximum-pool-size based on the number of application threads and database capacity. If you need full control, you can define your own DataSource bean and Spring Boot will back off from its auto-configuration.

speakable_v2.hook: Spring Boot wires a production-ready connection pool from three lines of application.properties — you don't write a single bean.

beats.text: Spring Boot's DataSourceAutoConfiguration detects HikariCP on the classpath and creates a fully configured DataSource bean automatically. You only need to supply the JDBC URL, username, and password. The pool starts, maintains connections, and handles cleanup without any explicit configuration code.

Auto-configuration exists because every Spring Boot app connecting to a database needs a DataSource — and the correct defaults (pool size 10, 30-second timeout, 30-minute max lifetime) suit most applications without any customization. Convention over configuration means you only specify what differs from the defaults.

items: Classpath detection: adding spring-boot-starter-data-jpa or spring-boot-starter-jdbc pulls HikariCP automatically
Minimal config: spring.datasource.url, spring.datasource.username, spring.datasource.password — that's it for a working pool
Tuning: spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size, connection-timeout, max-lifetime override the defaults
Override: define your own @Bean DataSource and Spring Boot backs off from auto-configuration entirely

beats.text: Our orders app sets spring.datasource.url=jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/orders_db and credentials — three lines. Spring Boot creates a HikariCP pool with 10 connections. We add spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size=20 for production because load testing showed 10 connections was the bottleneck. Spring Boot Actuator then exposes pool metrics at /actuator/metrics/hikaricp.connections. items: Manually creating a DataSource bean without @Primary when auto-configuration is also active — Spring finds two candidates and throws NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException
Forgetting to set max-lifetime below the database's wait_timeout — causes stale connection errors that only appear under production load or after the app idles overnight
Tuning maximum-pool-size without load testing — an oversized pool doesn't help and wastes database server connections

speakable_v2.cap: Three lines of application.properties give you a production-ready HikariCP pool. Add spring.datasource.hikari.* properties only when load testing or monitoring tells you to.
